title: Post Quantum Cryptography Roadmap
subtitle: A walk through the problem and the mitigation for new quantum computing attacks on existing cryptography

slides.title: Post Quantum Cryptography Roadmap
slides.lead: A walk through the problem and the mitigation for new quantum computing attacks on existing cryptography

slides.title: Disclaimer
body: I am an application engineer who focuses primarily on security, and am fascinated by the challenge Post Quantum Cryptography presents.
I did approximately 45% of my research with the assistance of AI.
This is an overall picture, in my opinion, of the work that we can anticipate over the next four years to be ready for quantum computers to break our current classical encryption.
And in a world of government funded state attackers, they will be using quantum machines to crack existing encryption as soon as it is possible.
I believe this knowledge should be shared so everyone can be prepared. We are all one part of a big happy family / worldwide compromise chain.

slides.title: The history
intro: The world needed a way to encrypt data with a publicly known key that only the holder of the special private key could decrypt.
The world needed a way to sign a piece of data using the private key that any public key holder could verify for authenticity.
items: Certificates were added and Public Key Infrastructure became widely used.
SSL, TLS and Message Level Encryption are used across the internet to secure our information.

slides.title: What is post quantum cryptography
body: A set of encryption and signature algorithms that cannot be broken by quantum computers, even those running Shor’s or Grover’s algorithm.
Uses lattice problems rather than factorization of primes.
Runs on classical computers, but is resistant to quantum computers.

c: ML-KEM – Key encapsulation
ML-DSA – Digital signature creation and validation
SLH-DSA – Stateless hash based signatures
FN-DSA – Small signatures with fast verification (draft / expected)

slides.title: The urgency of post quantum cryptography

body.t: The cryptography that protects our information across the globe has thrived on one single fact:
c: We can give everyone a public key they can use to authenticate and encrypt. The private key holder can decrypt or give a true signature.
And these keys would take longer than the real life of the solar system to crack.

body: But quantum computing will be able to crack the keys in a matter of minutes.
Post Quantum Cryptography uses new math that neither a classical computer nor a quantum computer can easily derive.
This cryptography can be implemented on classical computers today so we can be prepared for when the first quantum crack attempt comes.
Government sponsored state attackers will be attempting to crack these keys as soon as it is possible.

slides.title: The problem
body: RSA has been reliable for decades because multiplying two prime numbers is very easy (key determination), but factoring their product is extremely hard for classical computers.
This has allowed RSA and its alternatives, DH and ECC, to become deeply ingrained in everything we do.
Shor’s algorithm shows that quantum computers can quickly factor that product.
So we need new math to determine the keys in a way that is impossible for quantum or classical computers.
And we need to prepare to update every point in our systems that uses public/private key pairs for the protection, authentication and verification of our data.

slides.title: The attack vector is the key, not the payload
intro: The public keys used to encrypt data are secure enough that no current machine can reverse engineer the private key. It would take longer than the expected life of our solar system.
That private key is the secret to decrypt millions of information payloads.
body: A quantum machine could potentially crack a single private key in days or weeks, once that becomes possible – as early as the mid-2030s.
A single successful crack reveals the decryption key, not the payload.
Once that private key is discovered, every symmetric key it protected can be decrypted immediately.
Then each symmetric key can decrypt the information inside the protected payload.

slides.title: What are we doing about it
body: Hopefully by now we are paying attention.
And now we will begin to discuss what we can do about this problem.

slides.title: How does this impact business
body: Businesses should review and re-evaluate their cryptography and its implementation.
All cryptographic modules using asymmetric encryption will need to be modified or replaced.
All certificates in use will need to be renewed to the new Post Quantum Cryptography / classic key model.
Cryptographic modules for signing and verification of data will need to be replaced.
Symmetric encryption should be reviewed.
All hashing should be reviewed.
If you hear the term MD5 or DES, you should have already replaced it. Get on it now.

slides.title: Smaller business task list
body: There is a lot of information that may only apply to larger businesses running in their own datacenters.

body.t: The quick list of items to consider for smaller firms:
c: Server OS upgrades
Web server, SSL and SFTP updates
New cipher suite priority
New certificates supporting Post Quantum Cryptography
Network switch updates – mandatory Post Quantum protection of admin functions
Custom code that implements cryptography
Encrypted stored data
And don’t forget about your encrypted history: data backups, message retention, audit trail, old received files, etc.

slides.title: The current industry state
items: NIST approves three cryptographic standards for key encapsulation, public/private key encryption and digital signatures.
Operating systems are updated to support the Post Quantum algorithms.
The first Hardware Security Module vendors release Post Quantum algorithms in their modules.
Certificate vendors are working on releasing hybrid PQC / classical keyed certificates.
Core coding libraries are being released with Post Quantum Cryptographic algorithms.

slides.title: Tech concepts to know
items: The use of a publicly available key to encrypt data that only the private key holder can decrypt.
The use of a private key to sign a piece of data that any public key holder can verify for authenticity.
An irreversible way to transform data so it can be compared or looked up without decrypting the original.
The use of a single key to encrypt and decrypt data.
A machine that holds the key and performs encryption operations in a way that the key can never be retrieved.

slides.title: The tech dependency chain

body.t: Operating systems will need to support PQC algorithms.
c: Windows – built in to Schannel
Linux – OpenSSL 3.5 and later
Mac – CryptoKit
Android – verified boot and platform

body: Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) will need to support PQC algorithms.
Once certificate issuers have HSMs to protect their signing keys, certificates can be created that support dual classic RSA and PQC keys.

body.t: Cipher suites that support hybrid PQC / classical key encapsulation.
c: In many cases, these rely on the operating system cryptography.

slides.title: First point – protect any key exchange
body: If you are exchanging long lived keys over the internet, it is recommended you stop.
There are known compromises in our communication technology, and some sensitive traffic of high value could be intercepted for later quantum cracking.
Send keys or partial keys via a private, protected physical channel: either an entirely segregated network or, preferably, physical media.
Better – if you have the ability to use key derivation based on shared known inputs, that is far more secure.
Finally – if you have sent keys insecurely, make a plan to rotate those keys.

slides.title: Before you start

body.t: You will be making two sets of updates:
c: The first will enable Post Quantum Cryptography.
The second will allow only Post Quantum Cryptography.

body: Maintain a roadmap of what needs to be updated.
Automate as much of the updates as possible.
If you implement custom cryptography, do the work to modularize it for future replacement now.
Design your coding changes as if they will be weak and need replacement on day one. No defense is foolproof forever.

slides.title: Hardware Security Modules
body: If you have a hardware security module, contact your vendor for PQC supporting devices.
Also ensure it supports AES-GCM 256 for symmetric encryption.
For maximum key protection, consider allowing for key derivation components rather than relying on key exchange.

slides.title: Certificates
body: Know when hybrid Post Quantum certificates will be available from your vendor – the realistic timeline is 2027 to 2029.

body.t: There are two methods of certificate issuance:

c.t: Dual certificates for the same identity – one classical certificate, one PQC certificate
c: Supports maximum compatibility

c.t: Composite certificate – signatures from classical and PQC algorithms are merged into one composite signature
c: Tougher to forge

body: Plan on testing once those certificates are available.
If you self-issue certificates from internal systems such as Active Directory Certificate Services, HashiCorp Vault or Keyfactor, the support timeline may be different.

slides.title: Cipher suite order
body: Once new cipher suites are available, install them via updates to your servers and load balancers.
Enable these suites in your web server software, OpenSSL configuration, Windows Schannel and Active Directory policy, and prioritize them highest on the server order list.
Maintain a list of everything you touched. You will need to repeat the updates as PQC-only cipher suites become standard by 2030.
As you prepare for testing, you can temporarily modify the cipher suite order list to only support the PQC suites to test connectivity.

slides.title: Are cipher suites a hard cutover? No.
intro: You can support classical and hybrid PQC at the same time.
Right now, most major providers such as Cloudflare, Amazon and Microsoft already support PQC alongside current suites.
body: Your server has a list of cipher suites in its “preferred order”.
When a client connects, it sends a list of what it supports.
The server matches the client list to its preferred order list and picks the “most preferred” suite from the client’s list.
slides.footnote: This allows for a graceful transition without breaking connectivity.

slides.title: Does the PQC part of a cipher suite encrypt data?
body: This is a mixed question. Cipher suites are important in TLS, IPsec (VPN), point-to-point tunneling and more.
The encryption of data is done with a fast “symmetric key”.
The exchange of that key is done via Post Quantum key encapsulation, which is asymmetric encryption. It is far slower, so it is only used to protect the symmetric key.
So the quantum attack is not a compromise of the data; it is a compromise of the private key used to decrypt the exchanged symmetric key.
Once the attacker has the symmetric key, they can decrypt the data in the payload.

slides.title: Network hardware
body: Make a plan on day one to update your switch and router hardware to use Post Quantum protection when it becomes available.

body.t: The administrative functions of forgotten switches and routers have historically been a prime target for attackers.
c: These admin access points need to be protected against quantum attacks.

body: It is unlikely there will be an impact on the actual routing of packets, but it is recommended you test when it is time.
Any service mesh or gateway that performs TLS termination may require updates to properly support Post Quantum Cryptography.

slides.title: Your code
body: Do the programming languages that do your encryption support the right algorithms?
Do your programming library dependencies support the right algorithms?
Is your cryptographic code designed so that it is relatively simple to replace in response to a newly discovered weakness?
Implement a consistent abstract class or interface that code uses, then inherit your cryptographic wrapper from it.
Then wire up which module or modules are used at app startup. Configuring in code is slightly more secure than in a configuration file.

slides.title: Stored data
body: Is your stored data encrypted using quantum resistant algorithms?
Is it labelled so you can determine “which key” encrypted the data?
Would it be relatively easy to rotate a key should you need to replace an algorithm due to a newly discovered quantum weakness?
Is your code written so it can read “which key” was used to encrypt the data, use that key, and re-encrypt if the existing key has been marked obsolete?

slides.title: File transfer
body: If your business uses asymmetric encryption via technology like PGP, is it ready to use PQC?
OpenPGP has this on its roadmap and is actively testing.
Other vendors may be working on PQC, but rely on technology such as OpenSSL, an updated Mac CryptoKit or Windows CNG libraries being available on the OS.

slides.title: Message Level Encryption (MLE)
body: You may be protecting messages using a public/private key pair.
The code that processes decryption will need to be modularized to support current and Post Quantum algorithms.
You may need a configuration switch per entity to control which encryption is used.
You will need to plan to get new keys, and possibly support dual keys per entity.
Lastly, plan for when a Post Quantum algorithm also needs to be replaced due to a weakness.
Planning for when you are compromised, not if, can save a significant amount of time and money down the road.

slides.title: JWT, OAuth, SAML and other federated security
intro: Many of these will need updates to support Post Quantum signatures via ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
items: Will need signature updates, new key type parameters for PQC and new core library support.
Will need PQC or hybrid credential types.
And any similar technology will need updates to use PQC.

slides.title: Your history
body: We live in a world where we must assume that the deepest parts of our network will be compromised.
You have file backups, old file transfers, encrypted audit trails, old stored MLE protected messages and more that need to be retained for legal reasons.
That data will be quickly cracked by quantum machines before the legal hold ages out.
Make a plan to protect that data now. You can decrypt and re-encrypt, or dual encrypt with a new post quantum key, but it should absolutely be protected.

slides.title: The longer term
body: You will need to be prepared to fully switch to Post Quantum Cryptography only. The roadmap will be the same.
What we know about these algorithms is based on solid mathematics, but we cannot prove they are quantum proof until roughly 2030.
This means we may need to replay this roadmap to protect against undiscovered weaknesses once quantum computing becomes a reality.
Be prepared for when you are compromised, not if.

slides.title: What about already harvested and stored information
body: We know we already have a problem.
Telecommunications networks have been lurked on, and messages have been intercepted and stored by various governments.
This information can be decrypted once the private key has been derived by a quantum machine.
For most of us, this will be our financial information, which is already half available on the dark web thanks to other system compromises.
For some businesses, this will be other keys or secrets used to protect your systems.
For some entities, this will be important strategic information.

slides.title: What to do to protect harvested information
body: Implement PQC sooner rather than waiting until 2030. We expect the first crack of a private key as early as the mid-2030s, but the sooner we protect, the less harvested information there will be to crack.
Rotate your secrets and passwords, and evolve your information so today’s information is no longer applicable.
If clients have sensitive identifiers, consider rotating them after PQC is commonly used.
If you have sensitive strategic information and you are a valuable target, stop sending it over public networks.
Ideally, we will stop using identifiers such as SSN for verifying everyone.
And lastly, it might be wise to rotate the financial information you’ve used online in the next few years.

slides.title: So where do you start?
body: Begin by knowing your cryptographic debt and the cryptography that needs to change.
Take a pragmatic approach to walking through the inventory.
Then implement changes in waves, detailed in the next slides.

slides.title: Practical tips for the inventory process
body: Walk your network perimeter inward: web servers → load balancers → app servers → databases → backups.
Don’t forget the “soft” crypto: OAuth tokens, JWTs, SAML assertions, LDAP bindings, FIDO2 keys.
Tag each item with its dependency chain – OS → HSM → certificates → cipher suites – so you know what’s blocking what.
Document what you can’t change yet and set a calendar reminder for when vendor support arrives.

c: Catalog all cryptographic usage: asymmetric keys, certificates, cipher suites, HSMs
Identify obsolete algorithms (MD5, DES, SHA-1) and remediate immediately
Protect key exchanges – stop transmitting long-lived keys over public networks
Upgrade OS: Linux OpenSSL 3.5+, Windows Server 2025+, macOS Tahoe 26
Update HSMs and network hardware, and modularize custom cryptographic code
Budget for certificate renewals, server upgrades and code refactoring
Deploy hybrid PQC/classical certificates and cipher suites (ML-KEM, ML-DSA)
Update JWT, OAuth, SAML, VPN and MLE to support PQC signatures
Re-encrypt historical data: backups, audit logs, retained messages
Mandate PQC-only cipher suites and retire classical asymmetric algorithms
Validate quantum resistance as real quantum threats emerge (mid-2030s)
Maintain agility – design for future algorithm replacement, not if but when
